evidence: Bóna–Sagan 2005 Theorem 1.2 characterizes nondivisibility by one prime; Corollary 2.2 supplies p divisibility of interior entries for \(n=p^m\); Section 3 explicitly notes that higher valuations require additional analysis.
Classical Lucas and Kummer theorems yield digitwise divisibility and valuation tools for each binomial coefficient, but do not themselves state this minimized gcd over all nonendpoint Narayana peaks.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The old p-divisibility theorem proves the compulsory factor p but not that its exponent is exactly one, not absence of other common primes, nor the precise extra exponent at Fermat primes. The new global minimization and witnesses are needed. Generic Kummer-style valuation formulas are foundational tools, not a previously located explicit full gcd theorem.

originality.rationale: The closest fully examined archival source Bóna–Sagan 2005, arXiv:math/0505382, characterizes divisibility by a prime and gives interior p-divisibility for rows \(n=p^m\). It neither states the entire gcd in prime rows nor fixes the valuation of its extra factor 2 at Fermat primes. OEIS A001263 lists entries and A335965 counts odd entries; neither supplies the prime-row gcd classification. Targeted full-statement searches found no equivalent covering result; the inaccessible full text of the less-direct Eu–Liu–Yeh article is retained as residual risk, not claimed to be eliminated.
residual_risks: A hidden equivalent exact-gcd theorem may exist under another title or terminology; absence from searches alone does not prove novelty.
Eu–Liu–Yeh (2006) publisher full text was not materially inspected; accessible abstract does not identify a decisive covering theorem.
The result is a prime-row classification and must not be represented as a theorem for composite indices.

value.rationale: The interior-row gcd is the canonical maximal common modulus for Dyck paths of prime semilength with every nonextreme peak count. Previously established p-divisibility motivates the precise higher-power question. The complete answer detects Fermat-prime exceptions and determines exact common 2-adic exponents, not a user-chosen sample or a mere table recomputation. This sharp uniform arithmetic classification is useful when determining common divisibility constraints in enumerative refinements; no composite-row or unknown-prime existence statement is required.
